exercises.title: A stored procedure that's suddenly 40x slower
exercises.situation: A business-critical stored procedure that normally executes in three seconds is now taking two minutes. Explain how you would investigate the problem.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I would check the SQL query, see if there are any missing indexes, and try to make it run faster.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This jumps straight to a fix — indexing — without any diagnostic step first. It never confirms whether the slowdown is isolated to this procedure or part of a broader server issue, it doesn't name a single tool or piece of evidence it would actually look at, and it has no way to prove afterward that the fix worked. Indexing might not even be the right category of fix: this could just as easily be blocking, a stale statistics problem, or something that only shows up under certain parameter values — and this answer would never find that out.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd start by confirming whether this is isolated to this one stored procedure or part of a broader slowdown — if everything is slow, this isn't a query-tuning problem, it's a server-level resource issue, and that changes who needs to be involved and how urgent it is. Assuming it's isolated, I'd turn on the actual execution plan and compare it against what I'd expect: is SQL Server doing an Index Seek where I'd expect one, or has it shifted to an Index Scan? I'd check whether the WHERE clause predicates are still SARGable, since a function wrapped around a column or an implicit conversion can force a scan even with the right index in place. I'd run SET STATISTICS TIME and IO to get real numbers — CPU time, elapsed time, logical reads — and if elapsed time is running much higher than CPU time, that's a strong signal the bottleneck isn't the query's own logic at all, it's blocking: another transaction holding a lock this procedure needs. Beyond what this toolkit alone shows me, in a production environment with Query Store enabled I'd compare this execution's plan directly against its own historical baseline, which is the fastest way to tell whether this is a genuine regression or something that was always this slow under current data volume. I'd also check aggregated wait statistics to see what category of wait — locking, I/O, memory — is actually dominating, and I'd consider whether this is a cardinality estimation problem, where stale statistics led the optimizer to badly misjudge how many rows a step would return, or a parameter sensitivity issue, where the plan cached for one set of parameter values performs badly against very different values passed in later. Once I've isolated the actual cause, I'd apply the matching fix — update statistics, adjust an index, rewrite a predicate, or address the blocking transaction — and validate it by re-running STATISTICS IO and TIME before and after, so I can show the improvement with real numbers instead of just asserting it feels faster.

scopeBreakdown.label: Situation
scopeBreakdown.quickReference: A business-critical stored procedure has experienced significant performance degradation.
scopeBreakdown.explanation: A business-critical stored procedure that normally runs in three seconds is now taking two minutes — a roughly 40x regression with no known code change.

scopeBreakdown.label: Clarify
scopeBreakdown.quickReference: Determine when the degradation began, whether other workloads are affected, and whether relevant changes occurred.
scopeBreakdown.explanation: Before touching anything, confirm scope: is this one procedure, or is the whole server degraded? That single question determines whether this is a query-tuning problem or a server-resource problem, and skipping it risks tuning a query that was never the actual cause.

scopeBreakdown.label: Observe
scopeBreakdown.quickReference: Review Query Store, execution plans, wait statistics, blocking, and execution metrics.
scopeBreakdown.explanation: Gather evidence before forming a theory: the actual execution plan (seek vs. scan), SARGability of the predicates, SET STATISTICS TIME/IO numbers — and, going further than a single-query snapshot, Query Store history, wait statistics, and whether cardinality estimates still look reasonable.

scopeBreakdown.label: Plan & Perform
scopeBreakdown.quickReference: Identify the root cause and choose an evidence-based remediation.
scopeBreakdown.explanation: Only after the evidence points somewhere specific — a stale plan, a non-SARGable predicate, blocking, a cardinality miss, parameter sensitivity — choose the matching fix: update statistics, adjust an index, rewrite a predicate, or address the blocking transaction.

scopeBreakdown.label: Evaluate
scopeBreakdown.quickReference: Compare performance against the baseline and monitor for regressions.
scopeBreakdown.explanation: Re-run STATISTICS IO and TIME after the fix and compare the numbers directly against the baseline captured before changing anything, so the improvement is demonstrated with evidence, not a hunch that it 'feels faster.'

vocabulary.definition: The tree of physical steps SQL Server actually used to run a query — which operators, in what order, reading from where.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the ground truth for diagnosing a query — instead of guessing, you can see exactly what SQL Server chose to do.
vocabulary.example: I'd turn on the actual execution plan and check whether SQL Server is doing an Index Seek or an Index Scan on the main table.

lessonLink.label: Reading Execution Plans: Scans vs. Seeks

vocabulary.definition: A WHERE/JOIN condition written so SQL Server can use an index's B-tree directly, instead of having to evaluate every row.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: A predicate that looks fine but isn't SARGable — wrapped in a function, for example — silently forces a full scan even when the right index exists.
vocabulary.example: I'd check whether the predicate is still SARGable — a function around the column would force a scan even with the right index in place.

vocabulary.definition: SQL Server commands that print real measurements — CPU time, elapsed time, logical reads — for every query you run while they're switched on.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It turns 'this feels faster' into a provable before-and-after comparison.
vocabulary.example: I'd capture STATISTICS TIME and IO before and after any change, so the improvement is demonstrated with real numbers.

lessonLink.label: SET STATISTICS TIME and IO in Practice

vocabulary.definition: One transaction waiting for a lock that another transaction currently holds — normal, expected database behavior, not automatically a bug.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: If elapsed time is much higher than CPU time, blocking — not the query's own logic — is often the real bottleneck.
vocabulary.example: If elapsed time is way higher than CPU time, I'd check for blocking before assuming the query itself is inefficient.

vocabulary.definition: A SQL Server feature that automatically retains the history of a query's execution plans and runtime statistics over time, so you can see whether a plan changed and compare current performance against a real historical baseline.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the fastest way to prove a genuine regression — 'this plan changed on this date' — instead of guessing from a single snapshot. This T-SQL course covers writing and tuning queries directly in SSMS; Query Store is a server-level administration feature that goes beyond that scope, which is why it isn't one of this course's own lessons but is still worth knowing.
vocabulary.example: In a production environment with Query Store enabled, I'd compare this execution's plan directly against its own historical baseline.

vocabulary.definition: Aggregated data on what specific resource — locks, disk I/O, memory, CPU — sessions have actually been waiting on, tracked by SQL Server itself.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It tells you the category of bottleneck across the whole server, not just one query, which keeps you from tuning the wrong thing. Like Query Store, this is server-level diagnostic territory beyond what this course's query-writing focus covers.
vocabulary.example: I'd check aggregated wait statistics to see whether locking, I/O, or memory pressure is actually dominating.

vocabulary.definition: The optimizer's prediction of how many rows each step of a plan will produce, which it uses to choose join types and operators before the query even runs.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: A badly wrong estimate — often caused by stale statistics — can make the optimizer pick a plan that's a poor fit for the real data. This sits one level deeper than the execution-plan reading this course teaches: it's not just what plan SQL Server chose, but why it chose it.
vocabulary.example: I'd consider whether this is a cardinality estimation problem, where stale statistics led the optimizer to badly misjudge row counts.

vocabulary.definition: What happens when SQL Server caches a query plan based on the specific parameter values used the first time it compiled, and a later execution with very different values performs badly against that same cached plan.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's a common, non-obvious cause of 'this query is usually fast but sometimes grinds to a halt' that has nothing to do with indexing or data volume.
vocabulary.example: I'd also consider parameter sensitivity — a plan cached for one set of values performing badly against a very different set passed in later.

exercises.title: An SSIS incremental load that silently loses rows overnight
exercises.situation: A nightly SSIS package that loads new orders into the warehouse ran successfully last night — no errors, no failed tasks — but this morning three days' worth of orders are missing from the fact table. Explain how you would investigate.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd open the package and just run it again to see if it still happens.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This treats a silent data problem as if it were a crash to reproduce. The package already reported success, so rerunning it without checking anything first risks reproducing the exact same silent drop and learning nothing. It never looks at row counts anywhere in the pipeline, never considers that a component could be swallowing rows without failing, and has no plan for proving the eventual fix actually restores the missing data.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd start from the fact that the package reported success — that tells me this isn't an execution failure, it's a silent data-quality problem, which changes where I look. I'd pull the execution report from the SSIS Catalog and compare row counts per data flow component against a normal run, to see exactly where the count drops. A few usual suspects: the Lookup Transformation might be configured to ignore no-match rows instead of redirecting them to an error output, which quietly drops anything that doesn't match instead of failing or flagging it. A Conditional Split could be routing rows to a branch nobody's actually capturing. Or the incremental load's watermark logic — the WHERE clause that decides what counts as "new" — could have an off-by-one or time-zone bug that's excluding exactly the rows from these three days. I'd reproduce the issue against a copy of the source data for that window so I'm not debugging against production. Once I find the specific component dropping rows, I'd fix that one thing rather than touching the whole package, then validate by reconciling source row counts against destination row counts for the affected date range and confirming the SSIS Catalog's execution report lines up — not just rerunning and eyeballing that it "looks right."

vocabulary.definition: A separate path on an SSIS data flow component that redirects rows which fail or don't match, instead of letting them silently disappear or fail the whole package.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: If error outputs aren't configured, or a component is set to ignore failures instead of redirecting them, rows can vanish from a load with no trace.
vocabulary.example: I'd check whether the Lookup Transformation's error output is actually capturing no-match rows, or just discarding them.

lessonLink.label: Error Outputs on Data Flow Components

vocabulary.definition: A data flow component that checks each incoming row against a reference set of data and either passes it through, flags it as unmatched, or fails the row, depending on configuration.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Its no-match handling setting determines whether unmatched rows are quietly dropped, redirected for review, or cause a failure — a common place for silent data loss.
vocabulary.example: I'd check whether the Lookup Transformation is set to ignore no-match rows instead of redirecting them to an error output.

vocabulary.definition: A data flow component that routes each row down one of several output paths based on an expression, similar to a CASE statement for rows instead of values.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: If a condition routes rows to an output nobody is capturing, those rows disappear without any error at all.
vocabulary.example: I'd check whether the Conditional Split has a branch that isn't actually connected to anything downstream.

vocabulary.definition: A load pattern that pulls only new or changed source rows since the last run, usually using a watermark value like a date or an identity column, instead of reloading everything every time.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: A flawed watermark comparison — an off-by-one boundary, a time-zone mismatch — can silently exclude exactly the rows that should have been picked up.
vocabulary.example: I'd check the incremental load's watermark logic for an edge case that would exclude these specific three days.

vocabulary.definition: The SQL Server database (SSISDB) that stores deployed SSIS projects and records detailed execution reports for every package run.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Its execution reports show row counts and timing per data flow path, which is the fastest way to see exactly where a load's row count dropped.
vocabulary.example: I'd pull the SSIS Catalog's execution report to compare row counts per component against a normal run.

vocabulary.definition: The practice of comparing the number of rows read from a source against the number of rows that actually landed in the destination, for the same logical batch, to prove a load is complete.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the only way to actually prove a load didn't silently drop data — a package reporting success tells you nothing about completeness on its own.
vocabulary.example: I'd reconcile source and destination row counts for the affected date range rather than trusting that a clean rerun means the data's complete.

vocabulary.definition: A load designed so that running it again against the same source window produces the same correct result without creating duplicates — safe to rerun as part of fixing a problem.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Before rerunning any load to recover missing data, it matters whether rerunning it is actually safe, or whether it will double-insert rows that already made it through.
vocabulary.example: Before backfilling the missing three days, I'd confirm the load is idempotent for that window so rerunning it doesn't create duplicate orders.

exercises.title: A paginated report that times out for one department but not others
exercises.situation: A monthly sales report runs in a few seconds for most departments, but one regional manager's version of the same report times out every time she runs it from the Report Server web portal. Explain how you'd investigate.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just tell her to try running it again later, maybe the server was busy.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This blames an unverified cause — server load — without checking anything, offers her no real fix, and doesn't distinguish whether the slowness is specific to her data, her parameters, or something structural about how the report is cached or rendered. It also gives up the chance to actually prove what's wrong.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd confirm this is specific to her — same report, same server, just a different parameter value — rather than a general server problem affecting everyone, which immediately points toward her particular region's data volume or her parameter combination rather than infrastructure. I'd check which parameter values she actually selects; if her region has dramatically more rows than others, the dataset query itself may simply be heavier for her. I'd pull the report server's execution log data, which breaks a run's total time into data retrieval versus processing versus rendering — that tells me whether the bottleneck is the dataset query running against the warehouse, or SSRS processing and rendering a huge number of rows. I'd also check whether report caching or a scheduled snapshot is configured, and if so, whether it's only effective for certain parameter combinations — caching is specific to a given set of parameter values, so if everyone else uses common filters and she uses an unusual one, she may be the only person actually hitting a cold, uncached run every time. I'd check cascading parameters too, in case a dependent parameter is triggering an expensive query behind the scenes just to populate her dropdown. Once I know whether it's the query or the rendering that's slow, I'd fix that specific layer — an index or query rewrite for a slow dataset, or a caching/snapshot strategy that actually covers her case — and validate using the execution log again, comparing her timing before and after.

vocabulary.definition: The query definition inside a report that retrieves the actual data a report displays, separate from the report's visual layout.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: A report's performance problem often lives entirely in the dataset's query, independent of how the report itself is designed.
vocabulary.example: I'd check whether this dataset's query is simply heavier for her region's data volume than for other regions.

vocabulary.definition: Report parameters where one parameter's available values depend on the value selected in another parameter, each requiring its own query to populate.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: A cascading parameter can quietly run an expensive query just to populate a dropdown, adding time before the main report query even starts.
vocabulary.example: I'd check whether a cascading parameter is triggering an expensive query just to populate her region dropdown.

vocabulary.definition: A Report Server feature that stores the results of a report execution for a configured period so later requests reuse them instead of re-running the report from scratch.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Caching is specific to a given combination of parameter values, so a user with an unusual parameter combination may never actually benefit from it.
vocabulary.example: I'd check whether caching only helps common parameter combinations, leaving her unusual one running cold every time.

vocabulary.definition: The set of factors — dataset query cost, row volume, rendering format, caching, and server load — that together determine how long a paginated report takes to run.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Treating performance as one of several distinct contributing factors, rather than a single mystery, is what makes a targeted fix possible.
vocabulary.example: I'd work through the usual performance considerations systematically rather than guessing at one cause.

vocabulary.definition: The components — the Report Server, its databases, and the rendering pipeline — that together process a request from the moment it's submitted to the moment a rendered report is returned.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Knowing which stage of the architecture a request passes through helps localize where time is actually being spent.
vocabulary.example: I'd think about which stage of the Report Server architecture this request is actually bottlenecked in before assuming it's the database.

vocabulary.definition: Report Server catalog data recording, for every execution, how long was spent retrieving data versus processing and rendering it — a diagnostic resource that goes beyond what's visible in the report itself.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Without it, 'the report is slow' has no way to be broken into 'the query is slow' versus 'the rendering is slow,' which require completely different fixes.
vocabulary.example: I'd pull the execution log's timing breakdown to see whether her 45 seconds is data retrieval or rendering.

vocabulary.definition: The Report Server component responsible for converting a report's internal intermediate format into a specific output — HTML for the web portal, PDF, Excel, and so on.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Heavier rendering formats take meaningfully longer for large row counts, which can look identical to a slow query if you don't check which stage is actually taking the time.
vocabulary.example: I'd also check whether she's exporting to a heavier rendering format than the HTML view most other departments use.

exercises.title: A DAX measure that's right on one visual and wrong on another
exercises.situation: A "Total Sales" measure shows the correct company-wide number on a card visual, but on a table broken out by product category, the same measure's subtotal doesn't match what business stakeholders expect for one specific category. Explain how you'd investigate.
exercises.beginnerResponse: The formula is probably wrong, I'd just rewrite the measure until the numbers match.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This treats DAX debugging as blind trial and error with no theory of what's actually happening in the engine. It doesn't isolate whether the problem is the measure itself, the data model's relationships, or how row and filter context behave differently on a card versus a broken-out table — and rewriting a measure that isn't actually broken risks introducing a new, harder-to-find bug.
exercises.professionalResponse: Since the measure is correct in one context and wrong in another, I'd suspect the measure isn't actually broken — it's likely behaving correctly given the filter context it's being evaluated in, and that context differs between a single card and a table broken out by category. I'd first confirm this is isolated to one category rather than every row, which points toward a data problem specific to that category rather than the DAX logic itself. I'd check the data model's relationships and cardinality around that category's tables — a many-to-many relationship or an unexpectedly bidirectional filter direction can cause a fact row to be double-counted or filtered unexpectedly once you're sliced by category instead of looking at the whole table. If the measure uses an iterator like SUMX, I'd check whether context transition is happening the way I expect when the measure moves from table-wide evaluation to row-by-row evaluation per category. I'd isolate the problem by building a minimal test visual with just that one category and comparing it against a hand-written DAX query run outside the report — in DAX Studio or Performance Analyzer — so I can see the measure's actual output independent of any visual-level filtering quirks. Once I can reproduce the discrepancy in isolation, I'd check for duplicate fact rows tied to that category through a many-to-many join path, which is a common and specific cause of exactly this symptom. I'd validate the fix by comparing the corrected category subtotal, the other categories, and the company-wide card total against the source system's own numbers, not just against each other.

exercises.title: A dimension table where historical reports changed after last night's load
exercises.situation: After last night's load, several historical monthly sales reports now show a customer under their new sales region — even for months before the customer actually moved. Explain how you'd investigate.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just fix the region value for that customer and move on.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This addresses the symptom for one customer without understanding why historical periods changed at all, doesn't consider that this could affect every customer who's ever changed an attribute, and has no plan for actually restoring correct historical reporting — just "fixing" the current value, which is exactly the behavior that caused the problem in the first place.
exercises.professionalResponse: This pattern — historical periods retroactively reflecting a current attribute value — is a classic sign that the customer dimension is tracking this attribute with overwrite-style history when the business actually needs to preserve history for it. I'd confirm scope first: is this isolated to the region attribute on the customer dimension, or could other attributes or dimensions be affected the same way? I'd check how the dimension's ETL is classifying this attribute — if it's treating region changes as SCD Type 1, overwriting the existing row in place, then every fact row that joins to that customer, regardless of when it happened, now sees the customer's current region instead of the region that was actually true at the time. I'd check whether the dimension even has the infrastructure for history — effective-dated start/end columns and a current-row flag — or whether it's a flat table with no versioning at all. The real fix is reclassifying this attribute as SCD Type 2: when a customer's region changes, insert a new dimension row with a new surrogate key rather than overwriting the old one, and make sure the fact table's foreign key for historical rows points to the surrogate key that was valid for that customer at the time the sale happened, not the customer's current row. That also means backfilling: historical fact rows loaded before this fix was in place need to be re-pointed to the correct historical surrogate key, not just left alone, or the bug persists retroactively. I'd validate by rerunning the same historical monthly reports and confirming old periods now show the old region again, confirming new activity after the move correctly shows the new region, and spot-checking a few other customers who've changed attributes to make sure this wasn't an isolated case.

exercises.title: Explaining a slow stored procedure without saying 'the loop is slow'
exercises.situation: A junior developer wrote a stored procedure using a cursor to update rows one at a time, and it's taking twenty minutes against a table that should process in seconds. Explain, using precise terminology, what's actually happening and why, instead of just saying the loop is slow.
exercises.beginnerResponse: The loop is slow because it's going through each row one at a time, so I'd just tell them not to use a loop.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This names the symptom but not the mechanism — it doesn't explain why going row by row is actually slower, doesn't name the alternative pattern precisely, and gives the junior developer no real understanding to carry forward, just an instruction to avoid something without knowing why.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd explain this as a set-based versus row-by-row problem, which SQL Server developers often call RBAR — row-by-agonizing-row. SQL Server is built to optimize operations against entire sets of rows at once; a cursor forces it to process one row per iteration instead, which means the engine pays per-row overhead — opening and fetching from the cursor, evaluating the WHILE loop condition, running a separate UPDATE statement — multiplied by every single row, instead of paying that overhead once for the whole set. Each of those individual row updates is also its own logged operation inside a transaction, so the transaction log overhead multiplies the same way the row-count does. I'd rewrite the logic as a single set-based UPDATE statement, or a MERGE statement if it needs to insert, update, and delete together, so SQL Server's query optimizer can plan the whole operation as one pass against the table instead of thousands of tiny ones. To prove the difference rather than just asserting it, I'd capture SET STATISTICS TIME and IO on both versions and show the junior developer the actual before-and-after numbers — that's a much more convincing and durable lesson than just being told cursors are bad.

exercises.title: Describing an ETL package without saying 'it moves the data over'
exercises.skillTag: SSIS Vocabulary: Control Flow vs. Data Flow
exercises.situation: Asked to describe what a particular SSIS package does, explain it precisely — using the platform's own architecture and vocabulary — instead of saying it "just moves the data over."
exercises.beginnerResponse: It just moves the data from the files into the database.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This collapses two distinct layers of the package — orchestration and the actual row-by-row pipeline — into one vague action, names no specific components or transformations, and gives no sense of order of operations or error handling. It wouldn't help a teammate understand or maintain the package at all.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd describe the package in terms of its two distinct layers. The control flow is the orchestration layer: it sequences tasks like an Execute SQL Task that truncates the staging table first, followed by a Data Flow Task, connected by precedence constraints that determine order and what happens on success or failure. Inside that Data Flow Task is the actual data flow — the row-level pipeline — which pulls rows through an OLE DB Source, applies a Data Conversion to align data types, runs them through a Lookup against a reference table, and lands them in an OLE DB Destination. Under the hood, SSIS doesn't move rows one at a time between these components — it streams them through in fixed-size memory buffers, which is the data flow buffer architecture that makes this a genuinely different performance model from a simple loop. I'd also mention the event handlers configured to log failures, since that's part of how the package actually behaves in production, not just on a successful run. Describing it this way — control flow versus data flow, specific components, buffer-based execution — gives a teammate enough to actually maintain or debug the package, which "it moves the data over" never could.

exercises.title: Describing a dimension change without saying 'we just update the old record'
exercises.skillTag: Data Warehousing Vocabulary: Dimension Change Tracking
exercises.situation: Asked how the warehouse should handle a customer changing their sales region, explain precisely what happens to the dimension table and why — instead of saying "we just update the old record."
exercises.beginnerResponse: We'd just update the old record in the customer table with a new region so it shows correctly.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This treats "update in place" as the only option available, with no awareness that this choice has a direct, specific consequence for every historical report tied to this customer. It names no alternative, no keys, and no sense that this is actually a deliberate design decision rather than the obvious default.
exercises.professionalResponse: This is really a question of which slowly changing dimension strategy fits this attribute. If we just overwrite the region in place — SCD Type 1 — every historical sale tied to this customer will retroactively show the new region, which breaks point-in-time correctness for anyone running a historical report. If the business actually needs to see "what region was this customer in when this sale happened," the correct approach is SCD Type 2: insert a brand-new dimension row with a new surrogate key for the updated region, and leave the old row untouched with its original surrogate key. The fact table's foreign key for past sales keeps pointing at the old surrogate key — tied to the old region — while new sales after the change point at the new one. That depends on using a surrogate key rather than the customer's natural key as the fact table's join target, since a natural key alone wouldn't distinguish between the customer's two versions. If the business only occasionally wants to see both the current and immediately-previous value without full history, a hybrid SCD pattern — keeping a "previous region" column alongside the current one — might be enough instead of full Type 2 versioning. I'd make this decision explicitly with the business rather than defaulting to whichever is easiest to build, since it changes what every future historical report actually shows.

exercises.professionalResponse: I'd describe exactly which subscription mechanism is doing the work, because it changes what "everyone gets the report" actually means. If this is a standard subscription, every recipient gets the identical report, rendered with the same parameters, on the same schedule — fine if everyone genuinely needs the same view. Subscription scheduling then runs independently of both, often against a shared schedule so it doesn't need to be configured separately for every recipient. Describing it this way tells a teammate exactly what to check if a manager's region changes or a copy looks wrong — not just that "it's set up to email everyone."

exercises.title: Choosing between Import and DirectQuery for a 40-million-row fact table
exercises.skillTag: Power BI Architecture: Import vs. DirectQuery
exercises.situation: A stakeholder wants a Power BI report built on a sales fact table with roughly 40 million rows that needs to reflect near-real-time data. Explain how you'd decide the storage mode architecture for this report.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just use DirectQuery since they want it real-time.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This treats "near-real-time" as the only requirement and picks a mode without weighing what DirectQuery actually costs at that scale — every visual interaction issuing a live query against the source, no VertiPaq compression benefit, and real restrictions on DAX. It has no fallback plan if that turns out to be too slow, and no validation step.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd start by pinning down what "near-real-time" actually means to the stakeholder — minutes of lag or seconds — since that changes the right answer substantially. Import mode compresses the data into an in-memory model and is typically much faster for interactive queries, but it only refreshes on a schedule, so there's inherent latency between a source change and a report update. DirectQuery issues a live query against the source for every interaction, which can get genuinely real-time data but means query performance depends entirely on the source system, and at 40 million rows, a source that isn't tuned for ad hoc analytical queries could make the report feel sluggish. Rather than picking one extreme, I'd consider a composite model: Import mode with incremental refresh for the bulk of historical data, and a DirectQuery partition — or a small, frequently-refreshed Import partition — covering just the most recent window, so the report gets acceptable freshness without paying DirectQuery's query cost across the entire 40 million rows. I'd also check whether Power Query's transformations can fold back to the source as native SQL, since that affects whether DirectQuery performs reasonably at all. Before committing, I'd build a representative set of visuals against a realistic data volume and measure actual query times with Performance Analyzer, rather than deciding on storage mode from requirements alone.

exercises.title: Deciding whether a data load belongs in SSIS or a T-SQL stored procedure
exercises.situation: A new nightly load needs to pull data from three source systems, apply some business rules, and write to the warehouse. A teammate suggests just writing it as one big stored procedure instead of an SSIS package. Explain how you'd think through that architectural decision.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just use whichever one I'm more comfortable with.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This makes an architectural decision based on personal preference instead of the actual requirements, and ignores a basic constraint — whether a stored procedure can even reach all three source systems directly. It also skips over real differences in error handling, logging, and performance between the two approaches.
exercises.professionalResponse: The first question isn't preference, it's reachability: can a T-SQL stored procedure actually query all three source systems directly, using something like a linked server, or does at least one of them require a connection type — a flat file, an API, a non-relational source — that only SSIS's connection managers handle natively? If any source needs that kind of connectivity, a pure stored-procedure approach is off the table regardless of preference. Assuming SSIS is involved for connectivity, I'd still think about where the actual transformation logic should live. SSIS gives visual control flow and data flow with precedence constraints, built-in error outputs, event handlers, and the SSIS Catalog's execution reports for logging — all of which are faster to build and more visible to a teammate than hand-rolled TRY/CATCH and custom logging tables. But for the heavy, purely SQL-to-SQL transformation work between staging and the warehouse, a well-written T-SQL stored procedure, potentially built around a MERGE statement, running inside the database engine itself can outperform row-by-row SSIS transformations. So the common, pragmatic pattern is a hybrid: SSIS orchestrates the overall control flow — pulling from the non-relational source, sequencing Execute SQL Tasks — while the SQL-to-SQL transformation and load step from staging to the warehouse is a T-SQL stored procedure that SSIS simply calls. I'd validate this plan against the actual source systems' connection requirements before building anything, rather than assuming either tool is sufficient on its own.

exercises.title: Choosing the grain and schema shape for a new returns-tracking fact table
exercises.skillTag: Data Warehouse Architecture: Grain & Schema Design
exercises.situation: The business wants to analyze product returns. Explain how you'd architect the fact table and dimensions for this — specifically how you'd decide the grain and whether to normalize the product dimension into a snowflake or keep it a single denormalized dimension.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just make a returns table with a date, product, and amount column.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This skips declaring the grain entirely — one row per what, exactly? — which is the single most important decision in dimensional design and determines everything downstream. It doesn't consider reusing dimensions that already exist for sales, and doesn't address the schema-shape question the prompt actually asked at all.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd start by explicitly declaring the grain before designing any columns: one row per returned line item, not per whole return transaction, because analysts will need to slice by individual product and reason code, and a transaction-level grain would hide that detail. This makes it a transaction fact table — recording each discrete return event — rather than a snapshot of some state at a point in time. For dimensions, I'd reuse the existing conformed Product and Customer dimensions already built for the sales fact table, rather than building new copies, specifically so returns can be compared directly against sales using the same dimension keys — that's what "conformed" actually buys you. On the snowflake-versus-star question: I'd keep the existing flattened, denormalized star-schema product dimension already in use for sales, for consistency and query simplicity, rather than introducing a newly snowflaked product-category-subcategory structure just for this one fact table — mixing schema shapes for the same dimension across different facts creates confusion and extra joins for no real benefit. For the handful of low-cardinality return-reason and condition flags, I'd add a small junk dimension rather than storing raw text columns directly on the fact table, keeping the fact table itself lean. Before finalizing, I'd validate the design against real business questions — "returns by reason by region last quarter" — and confirm the declared grain and chosen dimensions can answer them without extra joins or an unplanned grain change.

exercises.title: Choosing SSRS or Power BI for a daily operational pick-list report
exercises.skillTag: Reporting Architecture: SSRS vs. Power BI
exercises.situation: The warehouse team needs a report that prints cleanly on paper, runs automatically every morning at a fixed time, and lands in a shared folder — with no interactive exploration needed. A stakeholder assumes it should be built in Power BI since "that's our BI tool now." Explain how you'd think through this.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just build it in Power BI since that's what everyone uses now.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This defaults to the newer or more popular tool without checking it against the actual requirements, and ignores that every requirement listed — precise print layout, scheduled delivery to a file share, no interactivity — points toward a completely different tool that already exists specifically for this purpose.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd walk through the actual requirements against what each tool is built for, rather than assuming the newer tool automatically wins. Power BI excels at interactive exploration — slicers, cross-filtering, drill-through, a dashboard someone browses on screen — but it has real limitations for pixel-precise print layout, and it isn't built around the idea of delivering a static file to a folder on a schedule. SSRS, by contrast, is purpose-built for exactly what's being asked for: paginated reporting designed to lay out and print cleanly, a Report Server that supports standard subscriptions to automatically render and push a file to a shared folder at a fixed time, and rendering extensions that handle formats like PDF well. None of that is a limitation of SSRS being "the old tool" — it's precisely the tool's intended purpose. I'd recommend building this specific report in SSRS, while keeping Power BI as the right tool for the team's interactive dashboards elsewhere — this mirrors exactly the pattern used in the Microsoft BI Capstone, where SSRS and Power BI run side by side against the same warehouse, each handling the kind of reporting it's actually built for. I'd validate this by confirming directly with the stakeholder that no one actually needs to interactively explore this particular report — if that assumption turns out to be wrong, the right answer could change.

exercises.title: Planning the architecture for a new stack before writing a single query
exercises.skillTag: BI Architecture Planning: Raw Data to Reporting
exercises.situation: You've been asked to build a full reporting solution for a new business area: raw source data needs to land somewhere, get cleaned and modeled, and ultimately support both a scheduled paginated report and an interactive dashboard. Explain how you'd plan the architecture before building anything.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just start building the Power BI report and figure out the data as I go.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This skips architecture planning entirely and jumps straight to the visualization layer, with no staging or warehouse layer in between and no plan for how the paginated report and the dashboard would share logic instead of each becoming its own separate, inconsistent extract of the source data.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd plan the layers before touching any tool. Raw source data should land first in staging tables with minimal transformation, just getting it into SQL Server reliably. An ETL process — likely SSIS — then cleans, conforms, and loads that staged data into a proper dimensional warehouse, with the grain and SCD strategy for each dimension decided explicitly up front rather than improvised later. Both downstream consumers — the SSRS paginated report and the Power BI dashboard — should query that same warehouse directly, rather than each building its own separate extract of the raw data, which is exactly how two reports end up quietly disagreeing with each other over time. I'd decide deliberately where business rules actually live: ideally in the warehouse or ETL layer, computed once, rather than duplicated separately inside the report's dataset query and the dashboard's DAX measures. I'd also plan deployment and scheduling up front — a SQL Server Agent job triggering the SSIS load on a schedule, followed by the report subscription and the Power BI dataset refresh, both timed to run only after the load actually finishes — and document the data's lineage from source through to each specific report, so a stakeholder asking "where did this number come from" has a real, traceable answer. I'd validate the whole plan by walking backward from each report's actual requirements to confirm the warehouse layer genuinely supports both consumers without duplicated logic, before writing the first query.

exercises.title: Explaining to a business user why a historical report just changed numbers
exercises.skillTag: Business Communication: Data Warehouse Schema Changes
exercises.situation: After a schema change to how a dimension tracks history, a business analyst notices that a report she's run every month for a year now shows slightly different historical totals than before. She's worried the data is broken. Explain how you'd communicate what happened and why.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd tell her the data's fine, it's just how the system works now.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This is dismissive of a legitimate concern, explains nothing about what actually changed or why, and gives her no way to verify the new numbers are more correct rather than just different — which is exactly the reassurance she actually needs.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd start by acknowledging her concern is completely reasonable — a trusted report changing numbers without warning should always get scrutiny, and dismissing that instinct would be the wrong response. I'd explain plainly, without a jargon dump, that the dimension used to track this attribute by overwriting the old value whenever it changed, which meant older historical rows ended up blended together under whatever the current value happened to be. The warehouse has since been changed to track that attribute's history properly, so older rows are now correctly attributed to the value that was actually true back then — this is a correction of a historical attribution bug, not new data corruption. I'd be specific about scope: this affects one attribute, over a defined date range, not the whole report or every number in it, so she can bound her concern instead of distrusting everything. I'd offer to sit down and walk through two or three specific historical records with her side by side — the old number, the new number, and the business reason for the difference — so she can verify the new numbers against her own knowledge of what actually happened during those months. I'd also proactively flag that any other report built on this same dimension will show a similar shift, so she isn't surprised a second time somewhere else and doesn't lose trust in a report that's actually fine.

exercises.title: Telling the business that this morning's numbers are a day old
exercises.skillTag: Business Communication: ETL Failures & Stale Data
exercises.situation: The nightly SSIS load failed overnight, so this morning's dashboards and reports are showing yesterday's data instead of today's. Explain how you'd communicate this to the business stakeholders who are about to start using those reports.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just fix the package and not say anything unless someone asks.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This treats silence as the default and risks stakeholders making real decisions on data they wrongly believe is current. It gives no proactive notification, no timeline, and conflates "stale" with "wrong" by not addressing the distinction at all.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd proactively notify the affected stakeholders before they start relying on the reports, rather than waiting for someone to ask. I'd state plainly what happened — the nightly load failed overnight, so today's reports are showing yesterday's data, not today's — and be specific about which reports and dashboards are actually affected, since not everyone who touches the warehouse is necessarily impacted. I'd give a realistic timeline for resolution rather than a vague "working on it," even if that timeline is just "investigating now, update in 30 minutes." I'd be careful to distinguish this clearly as stale data, not wrong data — the numbers from yesterday are still accurate, they're just not current, which is a very different situation from reports showing incorrect figures, and conflating the two needlessly erodes trust in the whole system. Once the load is fixed and has caught up, I'd send a second, equally direct message confirming the data is current again, so stakeholders know exactly when to resume trusting the numbers without having to guess. Separately, I'd flag to the team whether this failure should trigger a monitoring or alerting improvement, so a future failure is caught and possibly fixed before business hours next time, instead of being discovered by a confused stakeholder.

exercises.title: Telling report recipients their delivery method is changing
exercises.situation: To fix a reliability problem, you need to migrate several regional managers from individual standard email subscriptions to a single data-driven subscription. Explain how you'd communicate this change to the people who currently receive these reports.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just switch it over, they probably won't even notice.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This assumes a backend change is invisible when it could easily change the sender address, send time, or filename pattern the recipients are used to. It offers no explanation of the benefit to them, and no path for them to flag a problem — if their copy looks different after the switch, they have no context for whether that's expected or broken.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd notify the affected managers before making the change, explaining both what's changing and why it actually benefits them, not just that it's a backend convenience. I'd explain that we're consolidating several hand-maintained individual subscriptions into a single data-driven subscription, driven by a recipient and parameter table, which makes the report delivery more reliable and much easier to update the next time someone's region or email address changes — no more editing subscriptions one at a time. I'd be concrete about anything they might actually notice — a slightly different send time, a different sender address, or a changed filename pattern — so if they do see something different, it reads as an expected change rather than a new problem. I'd give them a clear, simple way to flag it if their copy looks wrong after the migration, and I'd personally verify at least the first delivery cycle myself rather than assuming success and moving on. I'd frame the benefit in terms they actually care about: fewer missed or duplicated reports, and much faster turnaround the next time their region list or distribution needs to change.

exercises.title: Validating that a Power BI report will actually hold up at full data volume
exercises.skillTag: Performance Validation: Power BI Refresh & Query Performance
exercises.situation: A Power BI report was built and tested against a sample of the data and performs great, but the production dataset is 50 times larger. Explain how you'd validate performance before this goes live company-wide.
exercises.beginnerResponse: It worked fine in testing, so it should be fine in production.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This treats a small sample's performance as proof at full scale, without naming any specific tool or metric to actually measure with. It doesn't separate refresh time from interactive query time, and has no plan if it turns out too slow once it's already live.
exercises.professionalResponse: I wouldn't trust the sample's performance to predict full-scale behavior, since model size, cardinality, and relationship complexity all behave differently once the data grows — a column that compressed well with a few thousand distinct values might not compress nearly as efficiently at full volume. I'd test against a realistic full-scale copy of the data, not the sample, and use Performance Analyzer in Power BI Desktop to measure how long each visual's actual DAX query and rendering takes at that volume. I'd separately measure scheduled refresh duration against the service's refresh timeout limits, and evaluate whether incremental refresh is now necessary instead of a full reload every single time. If DirectQuery is used anywhere, I'd confirm query times against the source at full volume specifically, not just the sample, since source performance doesn't scale the same way. If I find slow spots, I'd consider aggregation tables, simplifying the model, or pushing some logic back to the warehouse layer instead of handling it in DAX. I'd validate again after any changes, against the same full-scale dataset, before declaring the report ready for a company-wide rollout — not before.

exercises.title: Validating that an incremental load will scale as the source table grows
exercises.situation: An SSIS incremental load currently processes a few thousand new rows a night in under a minute. The business expects that volume to grow 20 times over the next year. Explain how you'd validate that this load will still perform acceptably as it scales.
exercises.beginnerResponse: It's fast now, so it'll probably still be fine later.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This assumes performance scales linearly, or doesn't scale as a problem at all, without checking any of the specific places a design tuned for the current volume could break down at 20 times that volume. It also proposes no actual way to test the projected future volume ahead of time.
exercises.professionalResponse: I wouldn't assume it; I'd generate or obtain a test dataset at the projected 20x volume and run the package against it directly, measuring with SSIS's own data flow row counts and timing, not just a stopwatch on the whole run. I'd specifically check the incremental load's watermark lookup logic — a Lookup Transformation doing a non-indexed comparison against the destination table is fine at a few thousand rows, but can become a real bottleneck at the higher volume if it isn't cached or properly indexed. I'd check the data flow buffer configuration, since the default buffer sizing tuned around the current volume may not be optimal once 20 times as many rows are streaming through the same pipeline. I'd also check destination table indexing — an index strategy that's fine for small nightly inserts can start causing lock contention or fragmentation at a meaningfully higher insert volume — and whether the fact table will need partitioning at the projected scale. I'd validate the whole thing end to end against the projected volume before declaring it future-proof, and document the exact volume it was actually tested at, so a future developer has a real basis for trusting "should scale" instead of just a feeling.

exercises.title: Deciding whether a slow report needs caching, a snapshot, or a query fix
exercises.situation: A paginated report takes 45 seconds to render every time anyone opens it, and several people open it throughout the day. Explain how you'd validate the right fix, rather than just turning on caching by default.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just enable caching so it's faster for everyone.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This picks a fix before diagnosing the cause, doesn't check whether the 45 seconds is actually query time or rendering time, and doesn't consider whether different users use different parameters — which would make caching useless for most of them. There's no plan to actually measure before and after.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd diagnose where the 45 seconds actually goes before picking any fix. I'd pull the report server's execution log data, which breaks a run's total time into data retrieval versus processing and rendering, since caching only helps the data-retrieval side and does nothing if the real bottleneck is rendering a huge table. If it genuinely is query time, and the underlying data doesn't need to be live to the second, both caching and a scheduled snapshot are reasonable options, and the choice between them depends on usage: caching is specific to a given combination of parameter values, so it doesn't help if different users pass different filters, while a snapshot works well when most users use the same or similar parameters. If the slowness traces to the query itself — a missing index, an inefficient dataset — I'd fix that directly first, since caching a slow query just delays who pays the cost rather than solving the underlying problem. I'd also factor in cache staleness tolerance: how much lag between the real data and what a cached or snapshotted report shows is actually acceptable to the business for this specific report, since that judgment call, not just speed, should drive the final decision. I'd validate whichever fix I apply by measuring the execution log's timing breakdown again afterward, comparing the data-retrieval and processing phases specifically against the original numbers.

exercises.title: Validating that a fact table design will hold up as it crosses a billion rows
exercises.situation: A fact table currently has about 40 million rows and queries run fine. The business is forecasting it will cross a billion rows within two years. Explain how you'd validate the design will still perform at that scale, rather than waiting to find out.
exercises.beginnerResponse: It's fine now, we can deal with performance later if it becomes a problem.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This defers a decision that's far more expensive to retrofit after the fact — partitioning an already-huge, live production table is much more disruptive than designing it in from the start. It offers no concrete validation plan and no mention of any specific technique relevant to warehouse-scale performance.
exercises.professionalResponse: I wouldn't defer this; the right time to validate is now, while changes are still cheap, not after the table has already grown past the point where retrofitting is disruptive. I'd evaluate table partitioning on the fact table's date key, so queries filtering to a recent window only scan relevant partitions instead of the whole billion-row table, and so maintenance operations like index rebuilds or archiving old data can target one partition instead of the entire table. I'd review the indexing strategy, confirming the right balance between a clustered index on the partitioning key and supporting nonclustered indexes for common query patterns, since over-indexing at that insert volume creates its own write overhead. I'd consider whether aggregate tables are needed for common rollup queries — daily or monthly summaries — so dashboards don't have to scan billions of detail rows for a number that's the same every time it's asked. I'd test actual, representative query patterns against a scaled-up or synthetic billion-row copy, measuring logical reads and elapsed time specifically, not just confirming the query still returns an answer. I'd document the validated design and the volume it was actually tested against, so the next scale milestone has a real precedent to build from instead of starting the whole evaluation from scratch.

exercises.title: Proving row-level security actually restricts what each role can see
exercises.skillTag: Performance Validation: Power BI Row-Level Security Testing
exercises.situation: You've configured row-level security on a Power BI report so each regional manager only sees their own region's data. Before publishing, explain how you'd validate that it actually works — for every role, not just the one you tested first.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I tested it with my own account and it looked right, so it should be fine.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This only validates a single role, and the tester's own account is frequently a report owner or workspace admin, which can bypass row-level security entirely — meaning the test may have proven nothing at all. There's no systematic plan covering every role, boundary cases, or re-testing after future changes.
exercises.professionalResponse: I wouldn't trust a single spot check, and specifically not one done with my own account, since report owners and workspace admins can often bypass row-level security entirely — testing that way can look successful while proving nothing about what a genuinely restricted viewer will see. I'd use "View As Roles" in Power BI Desktop, or an impersonated test account in the Service, to systematically validate every single role that's actually defined, not just one. For each role, I'd confirm the visible data matches that role's expected region exactly, including boundary cases — a manager who covers multiple regions, or a user who maps to zero rows, which should show nothing at all rather than an error or, worse, everything. I'd re-test row-level security specifically after any future change to the data model's relationships or filter direction, since a changed relationship can silently break which tables an RLS filter actually restricts, even if the DAX role expression itself never changed. If dynamic row-level security is used — where the role is driven by the signed-in user rather than a static assignment — I'd specifically test with multiple different signed-in identities, not just a role preview, since static testing doesn't always catch every dynamic-lookup edge case. I'd document the tested roles and scenarios so this is a reproducible checklist going forward, not just "it looked right" from one quick check.
